title: Own. Ship. Prove. The operator role

note.body:
An operator owns one region's Rumi, built around Teach Well, Improve, Learn.
[Haroon, in your own words: who is in the room]
Three of you start today. Those three ideas are what every change you make is for. When you are unsure whether something is worth building, ask which of the three it serves. If the answer is none, leave it.
(press)
Teach Well is the lesson plans teachers use in class. If a plan is too long, or hard to read on a phone, that is yours to fix.
(press)
Improve is coaching that makes the teaching better: the AI coach, and the people who watch lessons and give feedback.
(press)
Learn is what children learn, and how we know it. It is the hardest of the three to measure, and we come back to it twice today.
(press)
note.first_line: An operator owns one region's Rumi, built around Teach Well, Improve, Learn.

note.body:
Own. Ship. Prove.
Three words. I would like you to say them back to me at the end.
Own comes first: a region's teachers, and you plan for them with the team.
(press)
Ship. A hypothesis made live, worked out with the FSPs, the field team who visit schools. We ship on a hypothesis. An opinion, however confident, is not enough.
(press)
Prove. We measure against the hypothesis we wrote down before we shipped. If we cannot show it worked, we do not say it worked.
(press)
Each word answers a question you will ask this week. What do I own? How does work move? How do I know it worked? The rest of this talk takes them in that order.
(press)
note.first_line: Own. Ship. Prove.

note.body:
You own your region's teacher experience, and you plan it with the team.
[Privacy: say a colleague; say one region; no teacher, school or partner by name; no dollar figure.]
Owning it means it is yours to fix. You will get help, and the problem is still yours. Four things sit inside the ring.
(press)
First, the product in the teachers' hands: lesson plans, the coach, the quiz, the portal.
(press)
Second, the region's numbers, every morning. Since the end of August, those numbers are how an operator's work is judged.
(press)
Third, every bug report from a teacher or coach lands with you.
(press)
Fourth, outages. Since the retro on 26 October, each region handles its own, with the team's help.
(press)
Now the outer ring. You never plan alone. You coordinate and plan with your region's field team, the FSPs, and with the builders. They see things you cannot see from a laptop.
(press)
Nothing is built without teachers' input. Before anything is built, someone has listened to the teachers it is for, and ideally that someone is you.
(press)
So go to schools and talk to teachers, even before a region has launched. Sindh has no paid contract yet, and the trip is still worth it. The Sindh team already works this way: on 1 October they took a visiting reporter to a pilot school to meet the teachers. More on visits in a few minutes.
(press)

note.body:
Widen what's possible: find another reading of the problem, then prototype it.
This part of the job is easy to miss. A problem often reaches you with a fix already attached. Your part is to ask what else it could mean.
(press)
Say the team hears that teachers have no time, so the plans should be shorter.
(press)
Another reading: if time is the problem, could a lesson plan be audio, something a teacher listens to on the way to school?
(press)
A second case. We had no way to collect learning data, so we could not see what children were learning.
(press)
Then someone noticed that children can also do quizzes at home.
(press)
So the operator builds a prototype, and the teacher can send a quiz home to the class. Nobody asked for it. Building it anyway is part of the job.
(press)

press 7: moves to s05
note.body:
Ship on a hypothesis, not an opinion: work it out with the FSPs.
A team will often want to ship because someone feels sure. Your job is to ask for a hypothesis instead. The FSPs are the field team who visit schools, and they know what happens in classrooms. You iron out each hypothesis with them, and then you make sure the process is followed. A hypothesis has four ingredients.
(press)
One: what you see. The number, and where exactly it is low.
(press)
Two: why you think it happens. The teacher's reason, in their own words. Ask yourself: did a teacher tell us this, or are we guessing?
(press)
Three: what might help. The change, and the date teachers get it.
(press)
Four: if this, then that, because. One line you can say aloud. Then write down what result would prove you wrong, before you ship.
(press)
Here is one from September. What we saw: lesson plans ran to eleven to sixteen pages. Why: teachers read them on a phone. What might help: pages made for the phone. If we do that, then more plans get used. They came down to five to nine pages, and complaints fell.
(press)
And the quizzes. What we see: no learning data. Why: we had no way to collect it. What might help: a quiz the teacher sends home. If children take it, then scores come back to us and to the teacher.
(press)

note.body:
Your agents work overnight; you check their work in the morning.
You sit at the centre. Around you is a team of agents, a swarm. You give each one a piece of the work with a clear brief, and it gets on with it. A big job runs as a team with a lead agent, and this talk was built that way.
(press)
Each agent has an inbox. Agents pass each other short, plain messages: this part is done, please check that one. You can read every message.
(press)
So you can leave the swarm on overnight. You go offline and the work goes on. Brief it well before you sleep, because the brief is the main part of your work.
(press)
In the morning it shows you what it built, on staging. Staging is a safe copy of the bot, where the swarm can keep working without reaching a single teacher.
(press)
You look at it yourself. When you have seen it and you are happy, it goes to production, the real bot. That go is yours, every time.
(press)
And one rule with no exceptions. Before anything ships, test it end to end, the way a teacher would meet it: send the messages yourself on WhatsApp, or open the browser and run the automated tests. Passing unit tests do not count as a working bot. If you have not seen it work the way a teacher would, it does not ship.
(press)

Huddles are where you harvest context. Never skip one.
Every region has a daily huddle: the regional manager, the field team, the builders, and you. It is where you hear what the team is seeing, talk through specific hypotheses, and try other readings of a problem. Things often reach the huddle before they reach any document.
(press)
Two regions have new operators from today. Sindh goes to our new operator from the Moawin team, and Balochistan to our new operator from R&D.
[The third new operator's region is not on the screen, because no source names it yet. Say it only if it is settled.]
(press)
Skipping a huddle feels harmless on a busy day. It is how an operator falls out of step with the team, so keep every one. If you cannot be there, ask for the notes the same day, and read them before you build anything.
(press)

note.body:
Each week, one operator shows what they built and what they learnt.
The weekly operators' meeting is how we share learning across regions, and the operators take it in turns. The first twenty minutes belong to that week's operator: what they built and what they learnt. Then ten minutes of questions. In the last thirty minutes we read each region's weekly numbers together.
(press)
Here is the kind of thing that gets shared. Meta changed its pricing at the start of October, and our WhatsApp bill jumped. One operator moved the quiz into WhatsApp's in-app browser, a web page that opens inside WhatsApp and sends far fewer paid messages. The daily messaging cost fell to about a tenth. They wrote it up as a skill so others could copy it, and it is now going to every region.
[If asked how big the bill was: the written record shows one bill in the thousands of dollars, on 6 October. Any other figure is yours to give.]
(press)
A second. We used to make lesson plans as images. One operator rebuilt them as web pages for the phone, and eleven to sixteen pages became five to nine. They shared it at this meeting, and the other regions copied it.
(press)
That is what the meeting is for. When one region learns something, every region gets it.
(press)

note.body:
Visit a school once a fortnight. It is not optional.
[Privacy: no teacher, child or school by name; no story that points to one classroom.]
A visit is where you see Teach Well, Improve and Learn happen in a real room. Run the school-visits skill before you go. These pictures are from team visits, with faces blurred. In the classroom, look at the board and the lesson as it is taught. That is Teach Well.
(press)
Improve is the conversation with the teacher afterwards: what helped them today, and what got in the way.
(press)
Learn is the children's work. Look at what they wrote, what they got right, and where they got stuck.
(press)
Afterwards, agree with your regional team what changes. Bring what you saw to the next huddle, so the visit turns into something we build. Take pictures of boards and of the room from the back, and keep faces and school names out of them.
(press)

note.body:
Prove it: measure against the hypothesis, and the number shows in the weekly charts.
Proving starts before you ship. You write the hypothesis with the FSPs, and you write down what result would prove it wrong.
(press)
Then everyone measures against that hypothesis: you, the FSPs and the builders, all looking at the number you named before you shipped.
(press)
Where you can, run an A/B test: some teachers get the change and some do not, and you compare. Run it at a scale where the difference means something, and set the bar before day one. Our lesson-plan test in Islamabad in October ended in a tie, and the team said so.
(press)
And the number should show in the region's weekly report, the one named on the screen: the same charts, every week. Getting it there is the main goal of the operator team.
(press)
Here is what those charts look like, for Tanzania last week. Teach Well: the share of teachers who made a lesson plan each day, ward by ward. These are totals; no teacher is named.
(press)
Improve: the coaching score over eight weeks, set against what human observers scored. A hypothesis about coaching shows up here.
(press)
So the job, in one line: with the FSPs, a hypothesis. Ship it, measure it, prove it.
(press)
